P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: No. As an EU member state, Malta applies Article 63 TFEU, which prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments between EU countries and with non-EU countries. Banks still apply AML/KYC checks and may ask for the source of funds.

sources.title: Free movement of capital (European Parliament Fact Sheet)
sources.quote: Article 63 TFEU prohibits all restrictions on the movement of capital and payments between EU countries, as well as between EU and non-EU countries.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Very likely yes: Article 63 TFEU removes capital-movement restrictions, and EU banks and e-money institutions commonly offer foreign-currency or multi-currency accounts. No Malta-specific source on account rules was captured.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Before trading, a self-employed person submits a Declaration of Commencement of Self-Employment to Jobsplus, and registers for VAT under Article 11 (small undertaking, exempt) or Article 10 (standard). L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Individuals ordinarily resident and domiciled in Malta are taxed on worldwide income and gains. Those ordinarily resident but not domiciled are taxed on Malta-source income and on foreign income received in or remitted to Malta (PwC; Deloitte 2026). 2026 single rates: 0% up to EUR 12,000, 15% to EUR 16,000, 25% to EUR 60,000 and 35% above (PwC and Deloitte 2026 agree). Work done while living in Malta for foreign clients is normally Malta-source and taxable. Self-employed social security (Class 2) is 15% of the previous year's net income, capped at about EUR 4,362 a year for those born after 1962 (FreeMalta).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: National: a small undertaking can use the simplified Article 11 VAT registration. It charges no VAT and cannot reclaim input VAT, and since the EU SME reform it can also cover some transactions in other member states. The Article 11 limit is reported as EUR 35,000 a year for services (EUR 30,000 for other activities); above it, Article 10 registration with 18% VAT is mandatory. The standard VAT rate is 18%. Under the EU SME scheme, small businesses below a national threshold (at most EUR 85,000) can be exempt on domestic sales. Where services are taxed (EU-wide rules, illustrated by Irish Revenue guidance): (1) B2B, meaning services to business customers in other EU countries or outside the EU, are taxed where the customer is established, so no Malta VAT is charged; EU business customers self-account under the reverse charge. (2) B2C services to private individuals are, as a rule, taxed where the supplier is established, so Malta VAT applies once you are VAT-registered. (3) Exception: consultancy, legal, accounting, engineering, data-processing, advertising, licensing and electronically supplied services to private customers outside the EU are outside EU VAT, subject to 'use and enjoyment' rules. Electronically supplied services to private customers in other EU countries follow special OSS rules (not captured here).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies directly in Malta, supervised by the national data protection authority. It covers EU businesses and non-EU businesses offering goods or services to people in the EU.

sources.quote: These rules apply to both companies and organisations (public and private) in the EU and those based outside the EU who offer goods or services in the EU , such as Facebook or Amazon, whenever these companies request or re-use the personal data of individuals in the EU.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: EU consumer law gives a 14-day withdrawal right for online and distance purchases without justification: 14 days from delivery for goods, and from conclusion of the contract for services. Exceptions include personalised goods, perishables and date-specific services.

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: This means you can cancel the contract within 14 days without providing any justification (the "cooling-off period").

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: For goods this means 14 days from the date of delivery, for services 14 days after the day the contract was agreed.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: Part-time self-employment can qualify for a reduced 10% income tax rate, capped at EUR 12,000 a year, subject to conditions (e.g. also being in full-time employment, a pensioner or a student, per older guidance). Self-employed artists can opt for 7.5% on the first EUR 50,000 of net artistic income. Someone with a full-time job pays Class 1 only, with no additional Class 2 on part-time self-employment.

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw in local currency'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
